content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has been working to address the public health burden of kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis, VL) in the South-East Asia Region, where the disease is predominantly endemic in Bangladesh, India, and Nepal, with sporadic cases reported in Bhutan and Thailand. In 2005, a regional initiative was launched to eliminate kala-azar as a public health problem, with the goal of reducing the annual incidence to less than 1 case per 10,000 population at the sub-district level in Bangladesh and India, and at the district level in Nepal. Nepal has successfully maintained this target since 2014, while Bangladesh and India are nearing the goal. To formally validate the elimination of kala-azar as a public health problem, a standardized process is required. This document outlines the steps and criteria for such validation. Globally, an estimated 200,000–400,000 new cases of kala-azar occur annually, with 67% of these cases concentrated in Bangladesh, India, and Nepal. The disease is caused by the parasite Leishmania donovani, transmitted by the sandfly vector Phlebotomus argentipes, and follows an anthroponotic transmission cycle. In Thailand, the epidemiology of kala-azar remains unclear. The elimination initiative aims to reduce the disease burden among vulnerable and underserved populations, decrease case-fatality rates to negligible levels, reduce cases of post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (PKDL) by interrupting transmission, and prevent the emergence of kala-azar/HIV/TB co-infections. The main strategies include early diagnosis and complete treatment, integrated vector management, effective disease and vector surveillance, social mobilization and partnerships, and clinical and operational research. The elimination process involves three phases: the preparatory phase, the attack phase, and the maintenance phase. The attack phase focuses on implementing and monitoring strategies, including limited indoor residual spraying (IRS), intensified active case detection (ACD), early diagnosis, and complete treatment. The maintenance phase ensures that the annual incidence remains below 1 case per 10,000 population, with continued surveillance to prevent re-emergence. Since the campaign's launch, significant progress has been made in reducing case numbers and incidence rates. For example, in India, cases decreased from 44,533 in 2007 to 9,241 in 2014. Similarly, in Bangladesh, cases dropped from 9,370 in 2006 to 1,038 in 2014, and in Nepal, from 1,564 in 2005 to 280 in 2014. By 2014, Nepal had achieved the elimination target in all endemic districts, while 96% of endemic upazilas in Bangladesh and 74% of endemic blocks in India had reached the target. However, underreporting remains a challenge, and the true burden of the disease is not fully known. PKDL cases, which can act as reservoirs during inter-epidemic periods, have increased in Bangladesh due to active case-finding efforts, while few cases have been reported in India and Nepal, where active surveillance is not routine. Surveillance systems for VL and PKDL are not standardized, and active case-finding strategies require validation. The validation process for kala-azar elimination involves assessing whether a country has achieved and sustained the target of less than 1 case per 10,000 population. This requires a standardized, objective approach based on agreed criteria. The WHO Regional Office for South-East Asia (SEARO) will provide technical support to countries for validation activities. The criteria for validation include the presence of a comprehensive national strategic guideline for kala-azar elimination, effective surveillance systems, adequate access to diagnosis and treatment, integrated vector management, and functional cross-border coordination. Countries must also demonstrate sustained low incidence rates for at least three consecutive years. Operational definitions for monitoring and evaluation include the annual incidence of kala-azar, relapse cases, and PKDL cases. PKDL is defined as a patient with a characteristic rash, often starting on the face and spreading to other parts of the body, with positive diagnostic tests. Confirmed PKDL cases require parasitological confirmation through PCR, slit-skin smear, or biopsy. The WHO emphasizes the importance of capturing data from both public and private health sectors and documenting underreporting ratios. Surveillance systems must ensure exhaustive, sensitive, specific, complete, and timely reporting to reflect the true incidence rate.
